column3: The Evil Wedding of Stanton Drew
column5: During a Saturday wedding party at Stanton Drew, a pious harpist refused to play past midnight to respect the Sabbath, and a mysterious piper took his place. The piper, revealed to be the Devil, enchanted the dancers into stone with his tunes, and they remain so, waiting for him to return and release them.

In the village near Brent Tor, the Devil stole a newly built church during a dark autumn night, placing it atop the hill to mock the villagers. However, the villagers summoned a bishop who dedicated the church on the hill to St. Michael, resulting in the Archangel defeating the Devil and securing the church's position.

In Pentre-Cwrt, Carmarthenshire, the devil planned to drown the villagers by damming the River Teivy, but a clever cobbler thwarted his plan by convincing him that the distance was too great, causing the devil to abandon his effort. The pile of earth discarded by the devil still marks the spot today, known as Cnwc Coedfoel.

A tale from Llanarth tells of a night when the village was disturbed by mysterious noises from the church belfry, believed to be caused by the Devil himself. The local vicar confronted the Devil, causing him to flee in haste and fall among the gravestones, leaving visible marks on a stone still present today.

column3: The Welsh Origins of the Jack-o'-Lantern
column5: In Wales, the legend of the jack-o'-lantern involves Sion Dafydd tricking a devil multiple times, eventually escaping by clinging to an apple tree and transforming into a fairy. Sion's cleverness and the devil's stupidity are central to the tale, which ties his transformation to the notorious village of Rhiwgyfylchi, known for its wickedness.

In a tale set in Wales, the devil is said to have interacted with monks of Tintern Abbey by preaching from a rocky outcrop known as the Devil's Pulpit, only to be driven away by a surprise dousing of holy water. The superstition that chalked doorsteps can keep evil at bay underscores the narrative's theme of folklore and beliefs about the devil's presence in the region.

column3: The Devil's Doorknocker of Callow Pit
column5: Two men attempting to salvage a sunken treasure chest from a deep woodland pool managed to snag its iron ring handle before it slipped back into the depths, leaving behind a relic that eventually became a church door knocker. This heavy ring, carrying a legacy of folklore, now hangs on the entrance of Limpenhoe's parish church.
Local legend tells of ancient stone cairns near Aylburton where the Devil dropped his heavy load of rocks after being startled by a crowing rooster.

column3: The Shepherd and the Devil of Birdlip Hill
column5: A resourceful shepherd walking up Birdlip Hill outwits the Devil by tricking him into drinking a foul-tasting sheep medicine disguised as spiced ale. Consequently, the enraged Devil roars in agony and flees the area permanently.

column3: The Devil's Wheelbarrow and Cam Peak
column5: Fearing that the Severn estuary had become too godly, the Devil attempted to dam the waters with a heavy wheelbarrow of earth, only to abandon his plan and dump his load at Cam Peak after being tricked by a local cobbler.

column3: The Legend of the Devil's Chimney
column5: Angered by the region's Christian churches, the Devil sat atop Leckhampton Hill and hurled rocks at churchgoers until the stones rebounded, burying him underground beneath a crooked limestone chimney.

column3: The Devil's Door of St Andrew's
column5: At St Andrew's Church in Miserden, local folklore attributes supernatural significance to an ancient north doorway and an adjacent yew tree. Parishioners historically believed that malevolent entities passed through the church, while tradition holds that the threshold is used by the souls of the dead for their final journey.

column3: The Legend of the Ninety-Nine Yew Trees
column5: Local folklore dictates that exactly ninety-nine yew trees grow in the churchyard of St Mary's Church in Painswick, and any attempt by anyone to plant a hundredth tree will be destroyed by the Devil.

Built by the Devil in a single night, the ancient stone road between Acton Burnell and Cardington is haunted by Old Scratch, who appears at midnight on a white horse to judge and punish late-night travelers.

column3: The Card Player of the Boat Inn
column5: During a card game at a local pub, patrons discover that their mysterious and charismatic opponent is the Devil himself after catching a glimpse of his cloven hooves beneath the table.

column3: The Devil's Leap and the Crooked Spire
column5: The Devil, startled by the sudden ringing of church bells, leaped from the top of the parish church spire and warped its structure in his panic. This supernatural escape left behind the uniquely twisted steeple that still defines the town's skyline today.
The Devil drove a congregation from their place of worship near the River Clun through a relentless campaign of terrifying nocturnal noises, leading to the building's eventual conversion into a farm.

The Devil waged a relentless campaign of terror against the village church in Clunbury, disrupting sermons and creating terrifying nocturnal noises until the congregation fled in fear, leaving the building to become Chapel Farm.
When an attempt was made to haul the old church bells out of Colemere using twenty oxen, a boast invoking the devil caused the chains to snap, sending the bells plunging back into the mere forever.

column3: Wild Kynaston and his Satanic Steed Beelzebub
column5: The notorious outlaw Sir Humphrey Kynaston evaded the authorities with the aid of his supernatural horse named Beelzebub, whom local legend claimed was either a gift from a wizard or the devil incarnate. Operating from a cliffside lair on Nesscliffe Hill, he robbed the wealthy while protecting local villagers.

column3: The Fatal Curse of Ightfield Rectory
column5: A dismissed garden boy is followed by a persistent demonic shadow after his former employer curses him, leading to his mysterious death three days later.

column3: David and the Devil at Skyborry
column5: A farmworker named David repeatedly outwits the Devil after a chance encounter, eventually defeating him before leaving instructions for a bizarre and cunning burial.

column3: The Devil's Face on the Iron Bridge
column5: Old Nick is said to have cast his own silhouette into the ironwork of the historic bridge to watch over the people of Madeley Wood.
Two ancient standing stones near Market Drayton are said to have been dropped by the Devil to represent his ring and finger following a mysterious tragedy.

A mysterious stranger who acquired ungodly wealth abroad hosted a lavish Christmas Eve party at Minsterley Hall, only to be violently claimed by the Devil himself. The host was found dead with a pitch-black talon embedded in his eye after the estate was struck by a terrifying, fiery entity.

column3: The Satanic Steed's Leap at Montford Bridge
column5: When the local sheriff tried to trap the outlaw Wild Humphrey Kynaston by dismantling Montford Bridge, Humphrey's devil-gifted steed Beelzebub cleared the gaping chasm in a single bound.

column3: The Flying Devil of Much Wenlock
column5: After being acquitted of murdering his minister's daughter, a rejected quarryman invokes the devil's judgment upon himself and is subsequently killed by a machinery part known as the flying devil.

column3: Wild Kynaston and his Satanic Steed
column5: The notorious outlaw Sir Humphrey Kynaston acquired a magnificent black horse named Beelzebub after making a bargain with the devil himself. Riding this supernatural steed, he evaded capture through legendary leaps across Shropshire while operating from his ancestral castle and cave hideouts.

A picturesque spring along the ancient Roman road between Ruckley and Acton Burnell serves as a haunting ground for the Devil and his imps disguised as frogs. The largest frog, representing Satan himself, remains hidden at the bottom of the rocky basin.

column3: Hell's Bells: The Devil Visits St Alkmund's
column5: During a violent storm in Shrewsbury in January 1553, Satan scaled the spire of St Alkmund's Church and struck the church bell with such force that his claw marks were melted into the metal.
A group of rowdy drinkers in a Wem pub conjure the Devil in the form of a terrifying black bull, which is eventually banished by a clever clergyman using an everlasting candle.

column3: The Devil's Spadeful at Hangour Hill
column5: The Devil created Hangour Hill by shaking excess earth from his spade after digging the ancient Bichamditch. Beneath this barrow, a mysterious pair of silver gates is said to be hidden.

Builders attempting to construct a traditional building in Bodham found their work repeatedly torn down each night by Old Nick. In response, they redesigned the structure as a circular building, which completely confused the Devil and forced him to abandon his attacks.
A poor man who sold his soul to the devil in exchange for funds to build the local church outwitted the demon by dying just in time to be buried within consecrated ground.
A holy medieval rector famously captures and imprisons the Devil inside a leather boot. This legendary feat is immortalized in painted woodwork at a historic Norfolk church.

After human remains were improperly covered up rather than given a Christian burial in 1717, divine wrath caused the ground in Mossymere Wood to open up, swallowing ancient oak trees and creating a deep sinkhole claimed by the Devil.

On damp autumn evenings, a mysterious circlet of mist known as the Devil's Nightcap forms over the Devil's Punch Bowl in Croxton. Local folklore attributes this haunting atmospheric phenomenon to the devil's presence in the landscape.

Castle Eden Dene’s Devil’s Lapstone legend tells how the Devil, intent on sabotaging Durham Cathedral, flew through the ancient woodland gathering stones until his apron tore and a great rock tumbled from the sky. The stone still bears the scratches and blood he left trying to catch it—marks said to remain visible to anyone who seeks it along the Yew Tree Trail.

The fierce wind around Boston’s St Botolph’s Church is said to be the Devil’s breath, left over from the day St Botolph wrestled Satan so hard that the fiend puffed and blew a whirlwind that never died away. To this day, the gusts along the Stump are blamed not on the river or sea, but on that ancient, unholy struggle

Dorrington’s church sits half a mile from the village because, so the story goes, demons kept dragging the building stones uphill from the original site until the builders gave up and erected it there. Other local lore adds witches and the Devil himself—sometimes as a hare, sometimes as a white rabbit—haunting the lonely church on its mound
